learningObjectives.title: Cooking of food and heat transfer (conduction, convection, radiation)
Protein properties: denaturation, coagulation and gluten formation
Carbohydrate properties: gelatinisation, dextrinisation and caramelisation
Fats and oils: emulsification, shortening and aeration

questions.q: What are the three methods of heat transfer used in cooking?
questions.explain: The three ways heat moves during cooking are conduction, convection and radiation.

questions.q: Which statement best describes heat transfer by conduction?
options: Heat passes directly through a solid material by contact
Heat is carried by rising currents in a liquid or gas
Heat travels as electromagnetic waves through air
Heat is transferred only when food is frozen
questions.explain: Conduction transfers heat through direct contact, passing from particle to particle in a solid.

questions.q: When water in a saucepan is heated on a hob, hot water rises and cooler water sinks. Which method of heat transfer causes this circulation?
questions.explain: Convection currents form as heated liquid rises and cooler liquid sinks, circulating heat through the water.

questions.q: Which method of heat transfer is mainly responsible for cooking food under a grill?
questions.explain: A grill cooks by radiation, transferring heat as infrared waves directly onto the food's surface.

questions.q: An egg is fried in a hot metal pan on the hob. Which method of heat transfer moves heat from the pan into the egg?
questions.explain: Heat is conducted from the hot metal pan directly into the egg through contact.

questions.q: Convection currents can transfer heat through which of the following?
questions.explain: Convection occurs in fluids, so heat is transferred through liquids and gases such as water and hot air.

questions.q: Why are metals such as steel and aluminium commonly used for saucepans?
options: They are good conductors of heat
They are good insulators of heat
questions.explain: Metals conduct heat well, so they transfer heat quickly and evenly from the hob to the food.

questions.q: What is meant by denaturation of a protein?
options: The protein structure unfolds and changes shape
The protein absorbs water and swells
questions.explain: Denaturation is the unfolding or change in shape of a protein caused by heat, acid or agitation.

questions.q: When egg white is heated, it changes from a clear liquid to a firm white solid. Which process causes it to set?
questions.explain: Once denatured by heat, egg proteins coagulate, joining together to set the egg white into a solid.

questions.q: Coagulation of a protein refers to which change?
options: Proteins joining together to set or solidify
questions.explain: After denaturation, coagulation is when protein molecules bond together, causing the food to set.

questions.q: In ceviche, raw fish is soaked in lemon juice and its flesh turns firm and opaque without any heating. What causes this change?
questions.explain: The acid in lemon juice denatures the fish proteins, causing them to firm up and turn opaque without heat.

questions.q: Which two proteins in wheat flour combine with water to form gluten?
questions.explain: When wheat flour is mixed with water, the proteins gliadin and glutenin combine to form gluten.

questions.q: When egg white is whisked, it forms a stable foam. Why does whisking allow air to be trapped?
options: The proteins denature and stretch around air bubbles
The starch gelatinises around the air
The sugar caramelises to hold the air
The fat emulsifies the air into the liquid
questions.explain: Mechanical whisking denatures the egg proteins, which then unfold and surround trapped air to form a foam (aeration).

questions.q: What is gelatinisation?
options: Starch granules absorbing liquid, swelling and thickening when heated
questions.explain: Gelatinisation is when starch granules absorb liquid, swell and burst on heating, thickening the mixture.

questions.q: A flour-based sauce thickens as it is heated and stirred. Which process is responsible for the thickening?
questions.explain: The starch in the flour gelatinises, swelling and thickening the sauce as it is heated with liquid.

questions.q: Dextrinisation is best described as which change?
options: Starch browning when exposed to dry heat
questions.explain: Dextrinisation is the browning of starch when it is exposed to dry heat, breaking it down into dextrins.

questions.q: Onions are fried gently for a long time until they turn golden-brown and sweet. Which process gives this colour and flavour?
questions.explain: The natural sugars in the onions caramelise on heating, producing a brown colour and sweeter flavour.

questions.q: A slice of bread turns golden-brown when toasted under a grill. Which process causes the browning of the starchy surface?
questions.explain: The dry heat of the grill causes the starch on the bread's surface to dextrinise and brown.

questions.q: In mayonnaise, which food acts as the emulsifier that keeps oil and vinegar mixed together?
questions.explain: Egg yolk contains lecithin, an emulsifier that holds oil and water-based liquids together in a stable emulsion.

questions.q: Rubbing fat into flour when making shortcrust pastry gives a crumbly texture. What is this shortening effect caused by?
options: Fat coating the flour and limiting gluten formation
questions.explain: The fat coats the flour particles, preventing water reaching the proteins so less gluten forms, giving a short, crumbly texture.
